newsitem.title: PERU: Peru honors slain hostage crisis heroes.
newsitem.headline: Peru honors slain hostage crisis heroes.

text.p: Peru's euphoria at the explosive finale to its four-month hostage crisis gave way to grief on Thursday with the funerals of a captive judge and two soldiers slain in the battle with Marxist guerrillas.

Hailed as national heroes, the three were honoured with emotional ceremonies at their burials. President Alberto Fujimori joined hundreds of soldiers on a hillside cemetery for the burial of army Lt. Raul Jimenez and naval commando Juan Valer in side-by-side graves.
The two men's families and friends wept as military colleagues read tributes and Fujimori's son Kenji, for whom Valer was a bodyguard, watched stony-faced.
Also attending the ceremonies was Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived in Lima with congratulations for Fujimori on the assault that ended the four-month crisis.
"He is a hero to the fatherland, a pride for his wife, an example for youth," Fujimori said as his 16-year-old son wept and kissed the coffin.
"The soldiers died as all soldiers want to die, fighting for Peru," Lt. Razuri Esteves said. "You have been avenged."
Seven bullets killed Valer as he was leading Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, the rebels' prize captive, to safety across the roof of the Japanese ambassador's house.
In downtown Lima, the coffin holding Supreme Court judge Carlos Giusti was carried to Peru's Palace of Justice where families, friends and colleagues filed past and left flowers.

Giusti bled to death after being hit by a bullet in the leg in Tuesday's spectacular storming of the diplomatic residence where the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas had held 72 hostages for 126 days.
The bodies of the 14 rebels, felled by bombs and gunfire in a 40-minute battle, were taken to a Lima morgue to be collected by their families.

Although praise flooded in from around the world for the elite troops who rescued the VIP hostages, pressure grew on Fujimori's government to reveal exactly how Giusti died. There was speculation he may have been hit accidentally by a military bullet during an otherwise clinically executed operation that was compared with Israel's legendary 1976 raid to free hijack victims in Entebbe, Uganda.

The president of the Lima chamber of lawyers, Vladimir Paz de la Barra, calling for an investigation, said it was strange a tourniquet was not applied to Giusti's bleeding leg. "I think these cases should be clarified," Paz de la Barra said.

Legislators rose to their feet, sang the national anthem and shouted "Long Live Peru!" as the five congressmen among the released hostages returned to their seats. "I want to welcome them and salute the integrity shown in four months of captivity," Congress President Victor Joy Way said.

Japan, whose two dozen nationals were all unharmed in the operation, was full of praise for Fujimori's handling of the crisis despite not being consulted before the attack on what was legally its territory. Ikeda, whose 100-strong delegation included 27 police officers, six members of a medical team and 10 relatives of freed Japanese captives, passed on Tokyo's thanks to Fujimori and heard firsthand about the daring raid.

Tokyo had consistently urged Fujimori to seek a peaceful end to the standoff and had sent Ikeda to Peru in the early days of the crisis to urge restraint. After meeting Fujimori and attending the funerals, Ikeda was to meet Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated Dec. 17 cocktail party stormed by the MRTA.

Fujimori's patience finally wore out when the MRTA decided to limit medical visits to the captives. With the hostages warned via an electronic device, and the rebels playing indoor soccer, commandos swarmed into the building from all sides and five tunnels where they had been waiting for several days.

MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini shouted: "We've screwed up! We've screwed up!" before he was killed on the mansion's staircase, the daily La Republica reported on Thursday. The two teenage girls among the guerrilla band shouted at troops to hold fire saying "We Surrender! We Surrender!"
But the order was shoot to kill. And, according to security force sources, the rebels were given coup de grace shots in the forehead to ensure they were dead.

The successful operation reversed Fujimori's popularity rating overnight, according to the polling agency Apoyo SA. A survey conducted the day after the raid showed his approval level shot up to 67 percent from 38 percent four days ago, the lowest level during his seven years in office.
The raid gave Peru's military one of the biggest victories ever in its 17-year war with leftist rebels, in which about 30,000 people have died.
